John Bunyan
JON BUHN-yuhn
proper noun
English surname likely from a Norman-French root for “a swelling” or “a cushion”; the given name John from the Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”

See also: John Bunyan

📖 Biblical Definition

John Bunyan (1628–1688), the Bedford tinker turned Particular Baptist preacher, stands among the brightest witnesses God raised from the lowly. Unlettered by the world’s reckoning, he was schooled in the school of Christ through deep conviction of sin, recounted in Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, where the LORD brought him from terror to settled assurance in free grace. Refusing to silence his preaching at the crown’s command, he was imprisoned in Bedford gaol for twelve years rather than promise to cease declaring the gospel. There, in confinement, he penned The Pilgrim’s Progress, the allegory of Christian’s journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City—a book that, under God, has carried the way of salvation to more souls than any volume save Scripture itself. His doctrine was thoroughly that of the doctrines of grace: man dead in trespasses, sovereign election, the all-sufficiency of Christ’s blood, and perseverance to the end. Bunyan did not soften the narrow gate nor the burden that only the cross can loose. His life answers the lie that learning or station qualifies a man to herald Christ; the Spirit equips whom He calls. He preached as a dying man to dying men, and his pilgrim still walks, bidding every reader flee the wrath to come and look to the One who bore it.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An English Particular Baptist preacher and tinker, imprisoned for twelve years, author of The Pilgrim’s Progress, the most widely read Christian allegory.

expand to see more

JOHN BUNYAN, English Nonconformist preacher (1628–1688), a tinker of Elstow near Bedford converted out of profanity and despair to assured faith in Christ.

Imprisoned twelve years in Bedford gaol for refusing to cease unlicensed preaching of the gospel.

Author of The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678), the allegory of Christian’s pilgrimage to the Celestial City.

Author of Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, the record of his own conviction and conversion.

A convinced Particular Baptist holding the doctrines of sovereign grace; he counted persecution gain for the sake of preaching Christ (Php 1:29).

📖 Key Scripture

2Ti 2:9 — "Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound."

Mat 7:14 — "Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it."

1Ti 1:15 — "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief."

Php 1:29 — "For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Bunyan’s pilgrim is now claimed by a vague cultural “journey” sentiment stripped of the gospel of grace that is its whole substance.

expand to see more

Bunyan’s great allegory is often invoked as a generic metaphor for any “spiritual journey” or self-discovery, the word pilgrim emptied of Christian’s burden, his flight from wrath, and his deliverance at the cross. But Bunyan wrote no parable of self-improvement. His Christian is a guilty sinner fleeing the City of Destruction, saved not by the journey but by the Crucified One at whose feet his burden falls away. To borrow the imagery while denying the doctrine is to keep the road and forsake the Saviour who is its end.

The lesson to recover is that the Christian life is pilgrimage through a hostile world toward a sure city, sustained by sovereign grace and not by the pilgrim’s strength. Bunyan’s pen, sharpened in prison, calls every reader to count the cost, take up the cross, and press on through Vanity Fair and the Slough of Despond to the gate that the Lamb has opened. The pilgrimage is real; so is the wrath fled and the glory sought.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The surname Bunyan is of obscure Norman-French derivation; his given name John carries the meaning “the LORD is gracious.”

expand to see more

John Bunyan — John from Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious,” fitting for the author of Grace Abounding.

Bunyan, an English surname of uncertain Norman-French origin, possibly from a root meaning “a swelling” or “a hump.”

His trade-name “tinker” marks a mender of pots and kettles, a despised itinerant craft of his day.

Pilgrim, from the Latin peregrinus, “a stranger, a foreigner,” one passing through a land not his own.

Allegory, from the Greek allos (“other”) and agoreuein (“to speak”), a speaking of one thing under the figure of another.

Usage

"John Bunyan preached the same free grace from the pulpit and from the prison cell."

"Generations of believers learned the shape of the Christian life from John Bunyan’s pilgrim."

"When pressed to promise silence, John Bunyan answered that he would lie in gaol till the moss grew on his eyelids before he would cease to preach."
